A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Legion mapper-generation work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and matchable despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original code-generation tests in Table 3, application-performance experiments in Figures 6–7, and feedback ablations in Figure 8.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds OpenTuner comparisons, iterative DSL-generation results, and prompting controls in Table 2 and Figures 4–6.

M1.justification: AutoGuide corresponds to v1's enhanced feedback: both use keyword matching to generate the same explanations and suggestions. The DSL constructs, Trace agent decomposition, optimization objective, feedback-update procedure, and retained code examples are unchanged. The Agent-System Interface framing does not establish a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Circuit, Stencil, Pennant, the same six matrix-multiplication algorithms, and the same ten mapping strategies. Replacing Cannon's with SUMMA in the feedback ablation changes the analysis selection within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates OpenTuner against Trace, OPRO, expert mappers, and random mappers in Figures 4–5; v1 only cited OpenTuner. Figure 6 also adds zero-shot and five-shot comparators absent from v1's feedback ablation. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces OpenTuner evaluation using execution-time feedback and a failure penalty, including a 1000-iteration comparison against ten Trace iterations. It also tests DSL generation with up to ten compiler-feedback refinements and adds one-generation zero-/five-shot controls. The retained Trace/OPRO experiments still use ten iterations.

E4.justification: v2 adds a search-budget analysis extending OpenTuner to 1000 iterations, tests whether compiler feedback repairs DSL-generation failures, and adds no-feedback controls to investigate iterative refinement. Its feedback ablation replaces Cannon's with SUMMA while retaining Circuit and COSMA. The generated-mapper case studies are retained from v1's appendix.

E5.justification: Both versions report five optimization repeats, ten random-mapper seeds, averaged trajectories, and shaded bands. The repeated-run counts and uncertainty-reporting practice are retained; additional comparator curves do not introduce a different statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds OpenTuner results, including throughput ratios of 11× at ten iterations each and 3.8× for ten Trace versus 1000 OpenTuner iterations. Table 2 adds 100% success for iterative DSL generation, and Figure 6 adds prompting-control and SUMMA ablation results. The original nine Trace/OPRO trajectories and generation-test outcomes are unchanged. New Section 5.2 text says three C++ compilation failures were fixed, although Table 2 shows four.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendix A.1–A.2's formal DSL grammar, mathematical semantics for split, merge, swap, and slice, and the derivation showing split/merge inversion. This substantially reduces the formal specification and reasoning, although the online-optimization formulation remains.

C1.justification: v2 makes the Agent-System Interface and generative optimization central contributions, explicitly claims the first application of generative optimization to system optimization, and adds prominent claims of finding better mappers than OpenTuner with far fewer iterations. The original expert-mapper speedups and reduction of tuning time from days to minutes remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the OpenTuner comparison as evidence for richer feedback and the prompting controls as evidence for iterative refinement. Its DSL explanation emphasizes the smaller semantic gap and declarative design, replacing detailed discussion of C++ contextual-dependency failures. The Circuit memory-placement and matrix-multiplication communication explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 removes extensive DSL/index-mapping reference material and the reproducibility statement specifying a 16,383-token limit, default temperature, and planned code release. It also omits the explanation of reimplementing and validating expert mappers in the DSL. Conversely, it newly specifies one evaluation node and describes OpenTuner's feedback and failure penalty. Agent templates and mapping examples remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the automated-code-generation discussion with a substantial agentic-framework discussion, adding works such as ReAct, AutoGen, and MetaGPT while removing several code-model references. Research positioning shifts toward generative optimization with rich feedback versus traditional scalar-feedback optimization, alongside the new first-application claim.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and much of the method narrative are extensively rewritten around the Agent-System Interface. The scientific-application and matrix-multiplication evaluations are consolidated, code-generation evaluation moves afterward, and appendix organization changes substantially.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws the overview and agent diagrams, merges the nine performance panels into Figure 4, adds the budget-comparison figure, and expands the generation table and feedback plot. The mapping illustration, code-length table, and optimization pseudocode move to the appendix, while several formal DSL figures are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens comparative evidence through OpenTuner and prompting controls and substantially improves the exposition. However, it removes formal DSL specifications and reproducibility details needed to inspect and reproduce the central approach, while introducing the three-versus-four compilation-fix inconsistency in Section 5.2/Table 2. These material empirical and presentation gains coexist with technical-completeness and reporting losses, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
